featured_reviews.name: AD M
featured_reviews.review_text:
I wish I didn't have to 'rate' this place. It's where families work and live. It's been around for almost 150 years.
It was interesting to see the way this laundry facility is operated, with the men doing the washing  [some by hand and some in the newer electric washers] and the women doing the folding and ironing.
The best part of visiting here is the children.  Bright children getting an education and sweet as can be. They were very impressive.
When you walk down from the platform overlooking the ghat, you are greeted by a man who offers to take you through the whole place for a donation.
I chose to do this and I was not disappointed.  It was truly fascinating how everyone here works together for the common good of the community.  Something that stood out to me was that despite the poverty and obvious hard work being done here, everyone was smiling, very friendly and kind. There were containers with plants in various locations that people were tending. Each door to the individual cement rooms the families live in had some pretty decorative items. People were clean. It was obvious they took pride in their space and themselves.
The way the laundry is hung by type of garment or linen creates a very visually appealing clothes line.
I spoke with some of the women and children that live there and they were all very kind and interesting people. I'm glad I visited.
If you think you may want to visit the inside, please be aware that there obviously is a lot of water on the ground and it can be deep and slippery. I wouldn't recommend this to anyone who cannot climb ladders or is unsteady/has a difficult time getting around.

featured_reviews.name: Vikas_sculptor
featured_reviews.review_text:
Dhobi Ghat, Mahalaxmi, Mumbai: A Unique Cultural Landmark

Dhobi Ghat in Mahalaxmi, Mumbai, is one of the city's most iconic and vibrant landmarks, known for its fascinating story and rich history. Established in 1890 during British colonial rule, Dhobi Ghat quickly became the hub for Mumbai's "dhobis" (washermen) who manually washed clothes for residents, hotels, and hospitals. Today, it stands as the world's largest open-air laundromat, featuring over 700 washing platforms, each with its own cubicle.

The Ghat became famous due to the sheer scale and efficiency of the manual labor performed here. Every day, thousands of dhobis and their families, mostly from Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, work tirelessly, washing, scrubbing, and hanging clothes to dry across vast stretches of clotheslines. Their skill, speed, and precision in managing the vast quantities of laundry have made Dhobi Ghat an iconic representation of Mumbai's resilience and work ethic.

The sprawling Dhobi Ghat is located near Mahalaxmi railway station, making it easily accessible by train—a popular route for tourists. Visitors can take the Western Line and alight at Mahalaxmi Station; from there, the Ghat is just a short walk away. The best time to visit is in the morning when the dhobis are hard at work, creating a symphony of sounds and movements that showcase this unique cultural aspect of Mumbai.

featured_reviews.name: Para Para
featured_reviews.review_text:
Honestly, I don’t understand why people visit Dhobi Ghat as a tourist attraction. I passed by the area during my time in Mumbai, and the experience was very unpleasant.

I didn’t go inside — I just walked past — but even from the outside, the place looked very dirty and chaotic. The smell in the area was extremely strong and unpleasant, which made it hard to stay nearby for more than a minute.

While I respect the hard work of the people who work there, I personally don’t see the appeal of visiting this place as a tourist. It felt more like an uncomfortable stop than something interesting or meaningful to explore.

If you’re sensitive to smells or looking for something cultural and enjoyable, I would not recommend adding Dhobi Ghat to your itinerary.
